name: JAX
title: What Happens When You Run JAX? jit, XLA, StableHLO, PJRT | Language Lineage
h1: What Actually Happens When You Run JAX Code?
description: Trace JAX from Python to the device: op-by-op dispatch vs jax.jit, through jaxpr, StableHLO, the XLA compiler, LLVM or Triton, and the PJRT runtime, with sources.
og_subtitle: Python → jaxpr → StableHLO → XLA → LLVM / Triton → PJRT → CPU · GPU · TPU
verified_against: the JAX documentation (About, Just-in-time compilation, Ahead-of-time lowering) and the OpenXLA documentation (XLA architecture, XLA:GPU architecture, PJRT)
scope: Documented paths for one JAX program run without jit and with jax.jit, on a CPU, an NVIDIA GPU, or a TPU. Multi-device sharding, Pallas kernels, AMD GPUs, PJRT plugins for other hardware, and the internals of XLA's TPU backend are out of scope.
answer: Without **jax.jit**, JAX dispatches each operation to the device one at a time, as Python reaches it. With **jax.jit**, JAX traces your function into a **jaxpr**, lowers it to **StableHLO**, and hands the whole program to the **XLA** compiler, which fuses operations and compiles them for the target device. On CPUs and NVIDIA GPUs XLA generates code through **LLVM** (PTX for NVIDIA), uses **Triton** for some GPU kernels and NVIDIA libraries such as cuBLAS for others. Either way, JAX runs the result on the device through the **PJRT** runtime.

sections.heading: Where Python ends
paragraphs: Without jit, Python stays in charge of every operation: each jnp call is dispatched to the device on its own, so the compiler never sees more than one operation at a time.

With **jax.jit**, Python runs once to trace the function. From then on the computation is a jaxpr, then a StableHLO program, then an executable that XLA built for the device, and later calls with the same shapes reuse the compiled executable without running the Python body again.

sections.heading: How this differs from PyTorch
paragraphs: Both JAX and PyTorch's torch.compile capture a whole computation and compile it, and both can end up in Triton and LLVM on NVIDIA GPUs. JAX hands its program to XLA through a stable intermediate language, StableHLO, and runs it through PJRT; torch.compile captures an FX graph and generates kernels with TorchInductor. See [what happens when you run a PyTorch model](/ai/how-pytorch-runs).

out_of_scope_note: XLA's TPU backend is not described in the open-source documentation cited here, so this page shows that XLA compiles for TPUs without showing how.

stages.name: Your JAX code
stages.summary: Python functions using jax.numpy and other JAX APIs.

evidence.quote: Without jit, JAX executes operations (think jnp function calls) one at a time, dispatching each to the device as it's encountered.

stages.name: JAX
stages.summary: The JAX library. It traces and transforms your functions, and calls out to XLA and PJRT to compile for and run on devices.

evidence.quote: To manage hardware devices and memory, and for compilation to such devices, JAX calls out to the open XLA compiler and the PJRT runtime.

stages.name: jaxpr
stages.summary: JAX's own intermediate language: the traced function as a list of primitive operations, specialized to the argument shapes and dtypes.

evidence.quote: as a jaxpr: a function in JAX's intermediate language.

stages.name: StableHLO
stages.summary: XLA's versioned input language, a portability layer between ML frameworks and compilers. It is an operation set, not a programming language.

evidence.quote: Lower this specialized, staged-out computation to the XLA compiler's input language, StableHLO.
StableHLO defines a versioned operation set (HLO = high level operations) that provides a portability layer between ML frameworks and the compiler.

stages.name: XLA compiler
stages.summary: OpenXLA's machine-learning compiler. It optimizes the whole program, fusing operations, and generates code for the target device.

evidence.quote: The XLA compiler takes model graphs from ML frameworks defined in StableHLO and compiles them into machine instructions for various architectures.

It traces the function to a jaxpr (How transformations work: tracing) and hands the whole jaxpr to XLA, which compiles it into a single optimized executable, fusing operations, eliminating temporary arrays, and specializing for your CPU, GPU, or TPU.

stages.name: LLVM IR
stages.summary: XLA's CPU and GPU backends emit LLVM IR and use LLVM to generate native code.

evidence.quote: The CPU and GPU backends included with XLA use LLVM for low-level IR, optimization, and code generation.
These backends emit the LLVM IR necessary to represent the HLO computation in an efficient manner, and then invoke LLVM to emit native code from this LLVM IR.

stages.name: Triton IR
stages.summary: For some GPU kernels, XLA:GPU emits Triton IR instead of going straight to LLVM.

evidence.quote: XLA:GPU uses a combination of "native" (PTX, via LLVM) emitters and TritonIR emitters to generate high-performance GPU kernels

stages.name: cuBLAS and cuDNN
stages.summary: NVIDIA's libraries, which XLA:GPU calls for many common operations instead of generating code.

evidence.quote: For many common operations, XLA:GPU uses fast-performance libraries from NVIDIA, such as cuBLAS, cuDNN, and NCCL.
For every HLO instruction in the computation, XLA chooses whether to run it using a library linked into a runtime, or to codegen it to PTX.

stages.name: PTX
stages.summary: NVIDIA's virtual instruction set, produced through LLVM's NVPTX backend.

evidence.quote: The GPU backend currently supports NVIDIA GPUs via the LLVM NVPTX backend.
XLA:GPU uses a combination of "native" (PTX, via LLVM) emitters and TritonIR emitters to generate high-performance GPU kernels

stages.name: XLA TPU backend
stages.summary: XLA compiles for TPUs too. How its TPU backend generates code is not covered by the open documentation cited here.

evidence.quote: Compile the lowered HLO program to produce an optimized executable for the target device (CPU, GPU, or TPU).

stages.name: Compiled executable
stages.summary: The optimized program for one device and one set of argument shapes. Later calls with the same shapes reuse it.

evidence.quote: Compile the lowered HLO program to produce an optimized executable for the target device (CPU, GPU, or TPU).

stages.name: PJRT runtime
stages.summary: OpenXLA's uniform device API. Frameworks call PJRT; each device type implements it as a plug-in.

evidence.quote: PJRT C API is the uniform Device API that we want to add to the ML ecosystem.
XLA aims for interoperability across accelerators (e.g. by ingesting StableHLO as input) and PJRT offers extensibility through a plug-in device API.

stages.name: CPU
stages.summary: XLA's CPU backend supports several CPU instruction sets.

evidence.quote: The CPU backend supports multiple CPU ISAs.

stages.name: NVIDIA GPU
stages.summary: XLA reaches NVIDIA GPUs through LLVM's NVPTX backend and NVIDIA libraries.

evidence.quote: The GPU backend currently supports NVIDIA GPUs via the LLVM NVPTX backend.

stages.name: TPU
stages.summary: Google's Tensor Processing Unit, one of the devices JAX compiles for.

evidence.quote: Compile the lowered HLO program to produce an optimized executable for the target device (CPU, GPU, or TPU).
